newsitem.title: USA: Dollar debuts stronger in US as mark woes continue.
newsitem.headline: Dollar debuts stronger in US as mark woes continue.

text.p: The dollar began stronger in U.S. trade on Wednesday, extending its recent gains against an ailing mark in the wake of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's upbeat Tuesday Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.

Greenspan's positive take on the U.S. economy sent asset markets surging and added further fuel to an impressive dollar/mark rally which has been exacerbated by doubts about the strength of Europe's planned single currency.
In the wake of a fresh 71-month dollar peak of 1.8325 marks, set in overseas trade on Wednesday, dealers said they saw little reason to bet against a continuation of the move.
"It's a very very powerful move that is fuelled not only by dollar strength but by mark weakness which is even more profound," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer & Co.
"People are just liquidating their mark holdings against the dollar, against sterling, against the yen and the Swiss franc."
The dollar opened at 1.8280/90 marks, up from 1.8230/40 at Tuesday's close. The dollar also stood modestly higher at 115.10/20 yen against 114.95/00.
At the outset of trading, the mark was hovering near a two-year low of 62.93 yen and remained on the ropes against a host of European currencies.

Traders were eyeing the second leg of Chairman Greenspan's testimony to Congress, which is scheduled to begin at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT on Wednesday, and concurrent testimony from Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin, Fed Governor Laurence Meyer and New York Fed President William McDonough, who will speak to the House Banking Committee.
Although the content of Greenspan's speech will not differ from Tuesday's remarks, the question-and-answer session may provide new clues on Fed thinking, dealers said.
The dollar was expected to key off the stock and bond markets, as it did on Tuesday.
"People in the foreign exchange market are eyeing the long bond and the Dow closely," said Robert Fullem, assistant vice president at Natwest Bank.
"It's a very positive sign that we're sitting down below 6.5 percent on the long bond," he added.
Also encouraging to dollar/mark bulls was the conspicuous silence of the Bundesbank in the face of broad weakness in the German currency.
Although talk has surfaced that the Bundesbank could switch to a variable repo rate in order to send a signal about its displeasure with the weak mark, most traders dismissed the possibility.
"Germany has no reason to be disturbed (by the weak mark) unless there is inflation around the corner which there doesn't seem to be," said Fullem.
The Bundesbank will hold its last regularly scheduled council meeting before an upcoming summer recess on Thursday.
As U.S. trading began on Wednesday, the dollar stood higher at 1.4850/60 Swiss francs versus 1.4825/35 on Tuesday, and weaker at Canadian $1.3766/71 against C$1.3787.92.
The British pound was a tad stronger at $1.6800/10 versus $1.6798/08 and the Australian dollar was trading lower at $0.7361/66 against $0.7395/00.
